prompt: Why is having a wide tone-word lexicon important for advanced reading?
choice_a: Because longer tone words are always correct.
choice_b: Because all tone words mean roughly the same thing.
choice_c: Because tone words are required for vocabulary tests but not reading tests.
choice_d: Because you can spot an attitude but still pick the wrong tone word if you don't know the precise term.
feedback_b: They don't — that's why precision matters.
feedback_c: Tone questions appear constantly in MAP-style reading sections.
feedback_d: Correct. The skill is naming what you see, not just sensing it. A wide lexicon lets you pick the precise word.

prompt: Which of these tone words means "doubting, often quietly"?
feedback_a: Admiring is positive praise — opposite of doubting.
feedback_b: Correct. Skeptical is the standard word for quiet doubt — the kind of tone where the author isn't openly attacking but isn't accepting either.
feedback_c: Urgent is about time pressure, not doubt.
feedback_d: Nostalgic is about looking back fondly.

prompt: Read: "The official brushed off the complaints with a quick 'that's just how it is,' then changed the subject." The tone is:
feedback_a: Correct. "Brushed off" + changing the subject = dismissive. The official is treating the concerns as not worth engaging.
feedback_b: Reflective would mean thoughtful. "Brushed off" and "changed the subject" are not thoughtful.
feedback_c: Sympathetic would mean siding with the complainants. The official is doing the opposite.
feedback_d: Alarmed would be about danger or concern. The official isn't concerned — they're brushing past.

prompt: Read: "Fifty years later, the writer still wonders whether the bakery on the corner of her childhood street is open on Sunday mornings." The tone is:
feedback_a: Correct. Looking back fondly at a small specific memory from childhood is nostalgic.
feedback_b: No time pressure in the language — "fifty years later" is reflective, not urgent.
feedback_c: Nothing critical here — the memory is warm.
feedback_d: Reflective means thoughtfully looking back. The sentence is not only thoughtful; it is fondly drawn toward the past, which makes nostalgic more precise.

prompt: Read: "Without action this month, the damage to the coastline may be irreversible." The tone is:
feedback_a: Correct. Time pressure ("this month") + warning of irreversible consequences = urgent.
feedback_b: Despairing would mean without hope. The sentence calls for action — there's still a window.
feedback_c: Wry is dryly humorous. Nothing humorous here.
feedback_d: Sympathetic isn't supported — the focus is on the danger, not on whom we feel for.

prompt: Read: "The professor doubted, though politely, whether the new method was as effective as the marketing claimed." The tone is:
feedback_a: Scornful would be openly contemptuous. "Politely" rules that out.
feedback_b: Correct. "Doubted" + "politely" = quiet doubt. That's skeptical — the most-trapped tone at advanced levels.
feedback_c: Doubting is the opposite of admiring.
feedback_d: Indifferent would mean uninterested. The professor cares — they're questioning.

prompt: Read: "After everything that has happened, I have to wonder — somewhat ruefully — whether any of it was worth the effort." The tone is most precisely:
feedback_b: Alarm would be about danger; this is about effort.
feedback_c: Correct. "After everything" + "ruefully" + "any of it was worth it" signals thoughtful looking-back with a hint of regret. "Reflective and slightly regretful" captures the nuance.
feedback_d: The author is questioning value, not approving.

prompt: A passage uses these phrases: "supposedly", "in their words", and "although". The tone is most likely:
feedback_a: Admiring would use praise words, not hedging ones.
feedback_b: Correct. "Supposedly" + "in their words" + "although" are all skeptical signals — hedging verbs, distancing phrases, contrast words.
feedback_c: Urgent would have time pressure language.

prompt: A student writes "the tone is negative" on a test. The teacher marks it wrong even though the attitude IS negative. Why?
choice_a: Negative attitudes don't exist in tone.
choice_d: "Negative" is too broad — the student needed a more specific tone word like critical, skeptical, dismissive, scornful, or bitter.
feedback_a: Negative attitudes definitely exist — but "negative" alone is too vague to name them.
feedback_b: The grading is correct — the answer was just too imprecise.
feedback_c: Tone can be positive, negative, or neutral — many varieties.
feedback_d: Correct. "Negative" describes the general direction, not the specific tone. Advanced answers name the precise word.

prompt: Read: "The new policy is bold, ambitious, and — if the budget exists somewhere — perhaps even realistic." The tone is most precisely:
feedback_a: The aside about whether the budget exists undercuts full admiration.
feedback_b: Correct. The aside dryly questions the policy while keeping a lightly humorous edge; that is wry skepticism.
feedback_c: The tone is not hopeless or despairing; it is dryly doubtful.
feedback_d: The aside signals attitude, so the tone is not neutral.
